newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Would-be members want say in NATO - Russia charter.
newsitem.headline: Would-be members want say in NATO - Russia charter.

text.p: The Czech Republic, expected to be in the "first wave" of new NATO members, said on Monday applicants should be invited to take part in talks on a strategic partnership between the alliance and Russia.

"For us NATO allies, it is very important the debate with Russia not take place over our heads," Czech Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec said at a joint news conference after talks with Hungarian counterpart Lazslo Kovacs.

"It is important to have a system of consultations with the would-be members in this respect...It is our interest to have a statement and influence the position of NATO in these negotiations," he said.
NATO is mulling a charter setting out its relationship with Russia alongside plans for the alliance's expansion to embrace former Soviet Bloc members expected by the end of the century.

Hungary and the Czech Republic along with Poland are widely seen as the top candidates for NATO membership, but Russia has repeatedly attacked plans for tha alliance's expansion to Moscow's former communist allies.
Kovacs said it was important to keep Russia and other countries outside the alliance involved in questions on European security.
"It it very important to treat sensitively those countries, which will remain outside NATO," Kovacs said.
"It also is important how Russia gets into European security structures. From this perspective the format of the agreement between Russia and NATO is important," he added.
NATO Secretary General Javier Solana said in late October that no firm decision would come this year on the alliance's enlargement or future relations with Russia.
This followed soon after U.S. President Bill Clinton's call for NATO to accept some new members from the former Soviet Bloc by 1999 without naming which countries he would prefer.

Kovacs backed membership for Slovakia which has been repeatedly warned by the United States it could not be admitted unless it made more progress on democratic reforms and improved treatment of its large Hungarian minority.
"It would be very important to have Slovakia a part of Euro-Atlantic integration... it is in line with the interests of the Czech Republic and Hungary," Kovacs told reporters.
"It's important that there won't remain blank places in (NATO's) enlargement," he added.
Slovakia forms Hungary's northern boarder and lies wedged between Poland the Czech Republic and the countries of the former Soviet Union.
